newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - Norway rate cuts fails to weaken crown.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Norway rate cuts fails to weaken crown.

text.p: Norway's central bank said on Wednesday it would cut its key interest rates to rein in the strong crown, but the currency firmed rather than weakened following the long-awaited announcement.

Effective Thursday, the bank will trim the overnight deposit rate for commercial and savings banks to 3.5 percent from 4.0 percent. The overnight lending rate will be reduced to 5.5 percent from 6.0 percent.

The money market, which had been expecting the cuts for several weeks after a similar rate reduction on November 6 failed to deter the crown's rise, had discounted a 50 basis point reduction, analysts said.
They said the move was not enough and it would fuel inflation. The crown would continue to grow stronger against European currencies, they said.

"Clearly the economy does not need lower interest rates," Wike Groenenberg, a Salomon Brothers economist, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV). "As a matter of fact it is very harmful (for export industries)."
Oystein Stephansen at S-E Banken in Oslo said: "I still think the crown is undervalued. The cut does not alter the fact that the government (budget) and the current account have massive surpluses."
The crown has been appreciating for months because the oil-rich country's economy is booming and because short-term money market rates have been markedly higher than the German equivalent.
Central Bank governor Kjell Storvik said in a statement the crown had appreciated to the strongest level against European currencies since it was floated in December 1992.
The primary objective of Norwegian monetary policy is exchange rate stability, but the central bank has been anxious not to cut rates because this could drive up inflation and overheat the economy.
To counter the appreciation since the cut two months ago, the bank has bought foreign currency worth 38 billion crowns, including 15 billion crowns since the beginning of this year.
The statement said parliamentary guidelines put clear limits on the bank's scope for manoeuvre in the operational application of monetary policy.
"Against this background and in view of the extensive interventions that have been carried out, a reduction in interest rates is necessary to stabilise the exchange rate," it said.
However the crown, which stood at 100.64 on the inverse ECU index at 1430 GMT, half an hour before the cut, firmed following the announcement and stood at 100.50 points two hours later.
The three-month eurokrone swap rate, which was at 3.66 percent at 1430gmt, was down about 20 basis points, or below the deposit rate's new floor of 3.5 percent.
"The central thing will be to see how the market reacts when the Norwegian market is back again tomorrow," said Keld Holm, senior international economist at Lehman Brothers.

"But I don't think this will be enough. I think as the currency would not weaken people would see (the bank) cutting rates another time. We will have to see this strength going on for a month or two."
